deep_dive.title: BitSparse: Compact Activation Storage for ReLU Feed-Forward Networks
deep_dive.abstract: Reducing memory use in large language model (LLM) training is an ongoing challenge. Activation checkpointing saves memory by recomputation, while lossy compression changes the stored activations. The reemergence of sparse $\relu$ and $\relu^2$ activations creates a third opportunity: losslessly compressing the activation cache itself. We present BitSparse, a GPU-resident lossless compression format for sparse activations. Compression and reconstruction run in custom Triton kernels fused into an autograd function, shrinking the activation cache while recovering it exactly for the backward pass. Bfloat16 (BF16) and FP8 activations are supported. Optional sign-bit packing further increases compression up to close to the theoretical limit. We analyze its compression ratio and compare it to the theoretical optimum. BitSparse lowers per-token VRAM by 31\% and 30\% Modded-NanoGPT and Nemotron-H respectively, with overheads of no more than 1\% at practical sequence lengths. Additionally, a new preallocated buffer system avoids host synchronization during training when variable size tensors are allocated.

deep_dive.title: Efficient CPU-GPU collaborative MoE inference via Adaptive Expert Assignment
deep_dive.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reduce inference computation through sparse expert activation, but their large expert memory footprint often exceeds GPU capacity, making expert offloading necessary for memory-constrained inference. However, existing systems typically handle GPU-missed experts by either transferring them to the GPU, incurring substantial PCIe transfer latency, or executing them on the CPU, making the slower CPU computation the bottleneck. To address these limitations, we present \method, a CPU-GPU collaborative MoE inference system that adaptively assigns these missed experts to the CPU or GPU for efficient execution. By exploiting differences in expert token-loads, \method selectively transfers high-load experts to the GPU while executing low-load experts on the CPU. To minimize inference latency, \method adaptively adjusts expert assignments to balance the CPU computation path against the GPU transfer-and-computation path, allowing both execution paths to complete as early as possible. Extensive experiments on three representative MoE LLMs show that \method improves prefill speed by up to 51.9\% and decode throughput by up to 39.5\% over the strongest baseline across the evaluated batch sizes, with consistent gains under different GPU-memory budgets.

deep_dive.title: Breaking the Coupling: Efficient Concurrency Fuzzing for Linux Kernel Data Race Detection
deep_dive.abstract: Detecting data races in the Linux kernel requires exploring both the input space and the thread-interleaving space. Existing kernel concurrency fuzzers couple these two searches by exploring interleavings during fuzzing, often spending substantial scheduling effort on inputs with little potential to trigger real races. In this paper, we present a new concurrency fuzzing paradigm that decouples concurrent-input generation from thread-interleaving exploration, enabling expensive scheduling to focus on promising inputs.   To identify inputs that warrant targeted scheduling, we introduce May Race Pairs (MRPs), which represent conflicting memory-access pairs observed within a dynamically determined time threshold. Our framework first generates and executes concurrent syscall groups without controlled scheduling, collecting MRPs to guide further input mutation and identify schedule-worthy inputs. It then uses a separate scheduling instance to explore targeted interleavings and confirm real data races. To improve the effectiveness of both stages, we incorporate LLM-assisted semantic mutation for generating diverse syscall groups, backpressure-guided dynamic threshold control for balancing candidate production and scheduling consumption, and history-aware context recovery, context-aware interleaving scheduling, and candidate MRP prioritization for efficient race confirmation.   We implement our framework for the Linux kernel and evaluate it on eight common kernel modules in Linux 6.17. It discovers 187 unique real-world data races, including 59 harmful races. Under the same testing budget, our approach detects substantially more data races than existing kernel concurrency fuzzers, including SegFuzz and CONZZER. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of decoupling concurrent-input generation from interleaving exploration and concentrating scheduling effort on promising candidates.

deep_dive.title: RegoMender: A Multi-agent Framework for Automated Rego Policy Repair
deep_dive.abstract: Policy-as-Code (PaC) has emerged as a foundational paradigm in cloud-native systems. However, repairing Rego policies remains challenging due to their strict syntax, declarative semantics, and specific verification requirements. Existing automated program repair (APR) methods are mainly designed for mainstream languages and struggle to accommodate the unique policy logic and repair workflows of Rego. Thus, Rego policy repair remains a manual process driven by trial and error. To address this, we introduce RegoBench, the first automated Rego policy benchmark comprising 1,159 real-world defects, and propose RegoMender, a feedback-guided multi-agent framework. Collaborating via a shared blackboard and an atomic toolkit, RegoMender dynamically executes patching, rewriting, or rolling back, to resolve complex repair scenarios. Evaluated on RegoBench, RegoMender achieves syntactic and test-based semantic success rates of 82.9\% and 77.9\%, respectively, outperforming the strongest baseline by 13.4\%. Unlike other approaches whose performance drops in complex scenarios, RegoMender maintains effectiveness across single-step and chained repair tasks. Furthermore, it generalizes strongly across HCL and SQL and achieves an 86.4\% repair rate on 132 real-world CVE vulnerabilities, proving its robustness and practical utility for security.

deep_dive.title: Holistic Buoyancy-Driven Cloud Native Resource Management
deep_dive.abstract: Efficient resource management is a challenge in multi-tenant cloud environments as workloads compete for shared resources such as last-level cache and memory bandwidth, whose congestion can change dynamically as workload composition and resource demands evolve. Existing resource management approaches often rely on static resource requirements or prior workload profiling, limiting their ability to respond to changing resource contention as required in the cloud. In this paper, we leverage workload buoyancy, a runtime framework for capturing workload sensitivity to individual resources and application-level performance, to enable adaptive scheduling and resource management. We propose a holistic approach that incorporates buoyancy into workload scheduling, node-local resource allocation, and workload rescheduling throughout the workload lifecycle. We implement our approach as a Kubernetes-native prototype and evaluate it on a multi-node cluster using diverse cloud workloads under varying levels of resource contention. In a high-congestion scenario, our approach increases the percentage of workloads satisfying their SLOs from 7.74% to 87.8% on average compared with the Kubernetes baseline, while reducing resource congestion, the severity of SLO violations, and cluster fragmentation using limited rescheduling.

deep_dive.title: The Case for TPU-Accelerated Analytical Query Processing
deep_dive.abstract: Large-scale analytical query processing requires computing substrates capable of immense distributed scale-out. Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) perfectly embody this extreme-scale architecture, offering massive computational density and highly scalable optical pod-level interconnects. Despite these advantages, TPUs have so far remained largely unexplored for analytical database workloads. In this paper, we present the first comprehensive case for TPU-accelerated analytical query processing by running all the TPC-H queries entirely on the TPUs. We introduce Native TPU Accelerator (NTA) for analytical query processing, which provides hardware-conscious algorithm design and optimizations in JAX/XLA. By exposing the TPU's structural mechanics, we demonstrate how dynamic, memory-bound database operations can be rewritten into deterministic JAX programs. We engineer a suite of novel execution strategies that leverage both the TPU's TensorCore and SparseCore to trade sparse, unpredictable memory accesses for dense, hardware-aligned ones. At the core of NTA, a compiler uses catalog statistics to assign guarded static capacities and a hardware-calibrated local cost model to select a TPU-native implementation for each relational operator before JIT compilation.   We evaluate our system using the TPC-H benchmark. Taking full advantage of TPU slices and JAX distributed computing, we seamlessly scale our execution environment to run TPC-H benchmark up to Scale Factor 1000 (SF1000). Evaluated against a rigorous CPU ground truth (DuckDB), our native TPU accelerator achieves state-of-the-art performance, achieving a 7.0x single-device speedup over DuckDB at SF100 and a 68.6x speedup with 16 TPUs at SF1000 (1TB). The results establish TPUs not merely as dense neural compute hardware, but as a highly competitive, massively scalable substrate for the next generation of analytical query processing.

deep_dive.title: HydraLLM: Adaptive Width Slicing for Elastic Text and Vision-Language Models
deep_dive.abstract: LLMs and LVLMs are increasingly deployed across heterogeneous hardware, ranging from data-center GPUs to resource-constrained edge devices. Their fixed-size architectures limit the ability to reuse a single model across deployment settings with different compute, latency, and model-size targets. We introduce HydraLLM, an elastic MQA-based architecture. Its number of active attention heads determines the effective widths of the embeddings, attention projections, feed-forward layers, and the output head, forming a nested family of subnetworks within a single parameter set. We introduce a static-to-elastic conversion pipeline that, starting from a pre-trained model checkpoint, includes importance-driven weight reordering and stochastic subnetwork training with knowledge distillation. We extend this principle to multimodal inference through an elastic projection module whose output width follows the active text width. HydraLLM covers a wider range of active parameter configurations than FFN-only elastic architectures. With 75% of heads active, HydraLLM achieves 2.2 percentage points higher TriviaQA accuracy than a state-of-the-art nested baseline configuration which has 17.25% more parameters. With 50% of heads active, our multimodal model achieves a CLIPScore comparable to that of the 7$\times$ larger Gemma 3 4B model. With only 25% of heads active, HydraLLM increases token-generation throughput by 75.3% over the full-width configuration.

deep_dive.title: MailRail: Mitigating Incast Congestion with User-Space, Node-Based Flow Control
deep_dive.abstract: Irregular workloads, such as those stemming from Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, frequently induce severe incast congestion in large-scale parallel environments. Existing fabric-level congestion control mechanisms rely on reactive, link-level rate limiting that degrades overall throughput. While receiver-driven, credit-based flow control offers a proactive alternative, as process counts scale memory slots per rank fall below usable thresholds, rendering traditional rank-based accounting untenable. To address this challenge, we introduce MailRail, an out-of-order, asynchronous messaging framework, along with a novel user-space, node-based credit flow control system. By shifting credit accounting from individual processes to shared per-node pools, our proactive, fabric-agnostic approach maintains sufficient credit availability even as process density grows, enabling processes to dynamically utilize freed credits without waiting for receiver-side redistribution. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that node-based flow control achieves up to a 1132x speedup over unconstrained execution at an adversarial incast ratio of 4096:1 while adding minimal overhead on uniform workloads.

deep_dive.title: TideKV: Delayed KV Eviction via Layer-Wise Chunked Prefill for Memory-Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference
deep_dive.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is important for modern intelligent applications but remains constrained by peak memory during prompt prefill. Existing KV cache compression reduces decoding memory but typically requires full-prompt prefill to preserve global context, retaining a high construction peak. Online chunk-level eviction lowers memory earlier but selects before each layer has observed the complete prompt, potentially degrading cache construction and decoding. We present TideKV, an on-GPU cache-construction architecture using layer-major delayed eviction. TideKV processes all prompt chunks within each Transformer layer, retains full-prompt KV only for the active layer, and evicts at layer end. This schedule preserves full-prompt-aware selection while reducing activation and temporary memory. Experiments across multiple computing platforms show that TideKV preserves the inference quality and final cache size of the evaluated compression methods. At 64K on A100, it reduces the construction-time transient footprint by 83.89%. On RTX 4090, it increases time to first token by only 1.06% at 64K and enables 128K prefill. TideKV also completes 128K on Jetson, whereas matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory on both resource-constrained platforms. These results show that delayed layer-end eviction substantially expands feasible context lengths without sacrificing cache utility.

quick_skim.title: Data Center Load Accommodation under QoS and Checkpoint-Induced Frequency Security Constraints
quick_skim.abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence workloads is accelerating the expansion and grid interconnection of data centers (DCs). Existing data center load accommodation (DCLA) assessments primarily focus on grid and resource adequacy and often imply that greater workload flexibility always increases accommodable capacity. However, workload flexibility has a dual effect. Workload deferral and temporal shifting can alleviate network congestion, whereas synchronized checkpointing of training workloads can cause large and rapid load reductions, threatening frequency stability. Therefore, DCLA cannot be determined solely by grid adequacy. This paper develops an optimal DCLA method that jointly accounts for workload quality of service (QoS), checkpoint-induced frequency security (FS), and grid adequacy. First, a QoS-aware model characterizes workload-dependent flexibility while ensuring service feasibility. Second, checkpoint-induced FS constraints are developed for periodic and event-triggered power variations, with key frequency-security limits reformulated in algebraic form. Third, a two-stage lexicographic model is developed to maximize DCLA and minimizes the required energy storage (ES) deployment, and then optimizes system operation under the given DC and ES siting and sizing decisions. Case studies show that the proposed method avoids a 40.3% overestimation of DCLA compared with the grid-adequacy benchmark. QoS is the primary limiting factor, while checkpoint-induced frequency-security constraints become more restrictive as training workloads increase. These findings highlight that reliable DCLA should account for both its grid-support value and the associated QoS and FS risks.

quick_skim.title: PrairieFire: Igniting High-Throughput Updates in Large-Scale Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
quick_skim.abstract: Arrays of modern NVMe SSDs are approaching memory in terms of bandwidth while offering much lower cost per gigabyte. Hence, approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) for billion-scale vectors in applications such as recommendation, search, and retrieval-augmented generation increasingly runs on SSD-based systems. Unfortunately, due to the limited update throughput of existing SSD-based solutions, the indexed corpus cannot keep pace with continuous modifications to data and embedding models, thus hindering broader deployment across more scenarios and larger scales.   The bottleneck lies in CPU-intensive update paths, where foreground insertions incur frequent SSD accesses and background reassignments repeatedly relocate each vector, making high update throughput difficult to achieve even by exhausting available hardware. In this paper, using buffered updates and batched local rebuilds, we develop PrairieFire with cascaded adjustments, concurrency control, and CPU-GPU-SSD cooperation. These co-designs avoid frequent SSD accesses in foreground updates and heavy background reassignments, achieving high update throughput while maintaining excellent search performance.   Evaluations show that, compared with state-of-the-art systems, PrairieFire can sustain approximately 3-35x update throughput while maintaining approximately 3-5x search throughput simultaneously. It also achieves approximately 1.5-8.7x cost efficiency. PrairieFire has been deployed in RedNote's production environments for two months, improving business metrics by higher freshness without frequent index rebuilds.

quick_skim.title: GUMPIM: Unitary and Malleable Memory for Processing-in-Memory with Guaranteed PIM Pages
quick_skim.abstract: DRAM-based Processing-in-Memory (PIM) addresses the "memory wall" by executing computations directly inside main memory. However, memory interleaving and virtual memory limit contiguous data size visible to PIM units, constraining PIM task granularity. To mitigate this, existing PIM systems drastically isolate PIM memory or disable memory interleaving. These design choices, however, decrease the CPU memory bandwidth and introduce extra data transfer, leading to an additional "system memory wall" that must be resolved to realize PIM's full potential.   In this work, we propose GUMPIM, a PIM system that allows interleaved CPU pages and non-interleaved PIM pages to coexist in a Unitary and Malleable memory space with Guaranteed PIM page allocation. GUMPIM enables zero-copy during PIM task offloading and maintains CPU memory bandwidth while ensuring low PIM offloading overhead. First, we propose a dual-track memory management mechanism consisting of independent page allocation and address translation for CPU and PIM pages. Second, we design GUMPIM interface hardware on PIM-enabled DRAMs to provide a dynamic address mapping for the different data layouts of CPU and PIM pages. Third, we propose a PIM-assisted page migration mechanism that transparently migrates pages while preserving CPU access bandwidth, thereby enabling guaranteed and accelerated PIM page allocation. GUMPIM requires no changes to commodity DRAM standards; all hardware modifications are limited to the DRAM side, ensuring full compatibility with existing CPUs and enabling immediate deployment on current HBMx- and LPDDRx-based PIM platforms. Our results show only <0.1% performance degradation for CPU workloads on GUMPIM. For PIM workloads, GUMPIM reduces memory allocation and CPU-part computation times by 2.7x and 4.93x, respectively, yielding an end-to-end 2.3x speedup over a state-of-the-art baseline system.

quick_skim.title: KVCompass: A Discovery Plane for Internet-Scale Prefix Cache Sharing in LLM Serving
quick_skim.abstract: KV cache reuse is one of the most effective ways to reduce LLM inference cost, but today its benefits are largely confined to a single cluster. When a provider serves the same model across geographically distributed regions, each region may repeatedly prefill the same popular prefixes, wasting GPU time and increasing time-to-first-token (TTFT). Exploiting reuse across regions involves discovering which worker currently holds a reusable KV cache for each request's prefix. We show that this KV cache discovery problem is structurally harder than conventional object lookup. Unlike hash-placement mechanisms such as DHTs, where an object's location is a deterministic function of its key, KV caches are created on the workers that serve requests, and their holder sets change with subsequent requests and KV cache evictions. KV cache discovery therefore calls for decoupling KV cache identity from placement. We present KVCompass, a discovery plane for Internet-scale KV cache sharing. The discovery index supports variable-length prefix lookup with constant-time local table reads at the edge, allowing each request to be forwarded to the worker that best balances KV cache reuse against load and network distance. Evaluation includes a 64-worker geo-distributed simulation and a 14-worker three-continent real-machine testbed. Evaluation shows that KVCompass achieves $1.3-14\times$ lower P99 TTFT than the baselines, up to $3.7\times$ lower P99 end-to-end latency, up to $4.7\times$ the throughput, and a peak load factor within 2% of the Oracle floor.

quick_skim.title: EdgeKernelBench: Unified LLM-Driven Kernel Generation for Edge Backends
quick_skim.abstract: Recent works show that LLMs can generate kernels with strong performance on server GPUs. Edge deployment presents distinct challenges because the hardware is heterogeneous, the software stacks are fragmented, and the resource budgets are tight. LLM kernel generation across diverse edge backends has yet to be studied systematically. We introduce EdgeKernelBench, which combines a unified IR deployment framework with a hierarchical benchmark for edge workloads. The unified IR captures reusable computation, scheduling, and memory decisions and connects to each target backend through a compiler interface. The benchmark spans progressively larger program scopes, from individual operators to compact model graphs, across representative edge application domains. We instantiate the design with TVM as a reference compiler and validate it across heterogeneous edge backends. With a single generation attempt, the best model achieves 64.5% Correct@1 but only 25.5% Fast@1.0. This gap shows that functional correctness does not consistently translate into performance gains. We therefore introduce the Layered Edge Kernel Agent (LEKA), which organizes optimization through a layered IR. On the agent evaluation subset, LEKA achieves 43.5% Fast@1.0, compared with 13.0% for direct generation and 26.1% for Claude Code. LEKA and Claude Code use the same base model and optimization budget. Together, EdgeKernelBench and LEKA support unified evaluation and layered optimization of kernels generated by LLMs across edge backends.

quick_skim.title: Conjugate Compilation: Self-Improving Agentic Co-Compilation for Speculative Decoding
quick_skim.abstract: As LLM adoption surges, scaling model serving requires unlocking stranded GPU capacity alongside deploying more GPUs. Speculative decoding brings two models into the serving process: a small draft model proposes tokens that a larger target model verifies. Yet compiling these models individually leaves their shared execution outside the compiler's optimization boundary. We introduce CONJUGATE COMPILATION, which reframes speculative decoding as a cross-model compilation problem and jointly optimizes the draft and target models within their shared execution rather than treating each in isolation. Our key insight is that cross-model compilation should be informed by the measured performance of the co-located shared execution it produces: an optimization that improves a kernel in isolation need not improve the models when they execute together. To expand cross-model opportunities, we devise operand layouts that interleave blocks from both models within common tiles, co-locating GEMM and non-GEMM work while preserving their mathematics. We realize CONJUGATE COMPILATION through a self-improving agentic search system in which an LLM edits cross-model optimization plans using the compiler and GPU execution as its environment. quick_skim.title: PlaneZip: Lossless Bit-Plane Compression of Training Activations Offloaded over PCIe
quick_skim.abstract: Training under a device-memory budget relies on tensor rematerialization: an evicted activation is either swapped to host memory or dropped and recomputed. Because GPU compute has outgrown PCIe bandwidth, cost-model planners such as MegTaiChi, which charge a swap its full transfer time, almost never swap, and swaps that fill idle link time carry only a small fraction of the saved activations. Saved activations, however, are homogeneously typed arrays with bit-level redundancy beyond zeros, which lightweight bit-plane compressors can remove at line rate. We present PlaneZip, which compresses swapped tensors on the copy path and plans around the compression. Its codec picks, for every 128-byte block, the smallest of zero-value, delta bit-plane, bit-plane, and a new zero-masked bit-plane encoding. A per-tensor predictor reuses the ratio of the previous iteration, and the planner budgets link time in compressed transfer times. On activations captured from five models trained on real data, the codec compresses BF16 activations by 1.71x and FP32 activations by 1.39x (geometric means), against 1.18x and 1.20x for zero-value compression. In trace-driven simulation of a PCIe 3.0 consumer GPU and a PCIe 4.0 datacenter GPU at half the activation memory, PlaneZip cuts the rematerialization overhead by 47% and 31% relative to a bandwidth-aware planner without compression, and by 73% and 54% relative to MegTaiChi's cost model, with an estimated engine area of 0.036 square millimeters.

quick_skim.title: PACT: NVFP4 Data-Flow LoRA Fine-Tuning on Consumer GPUs
quick_skim.abstract: Fine-tuning language models on consumer GPUs is constrained by computation and memory. Although LoRA reduces trainable parameters and optimizer state, frozen projections remain expensive, and activations retained for backward can dominate memory usage. We present PACT, a LoRA fine-tuning system that accelerates frozen projections with native NVFP4 GEMMs while reducing quantization and dequantization overhead and limiting quantization error. To reduce activation memory, PACT reuses quantized RMSNorm outputs and saves gate/up activations in NVFP4 for backward. To limit numerical error, it preserves BF16 inputs for forward nonlinear operations and calibrates frozen weights offline using GPTQ adapted to NVFP4 scales and quantized activations. Fused nonlinear kernels and cached forward and backward weight layouts reduce quantization and dequantization overhead. Evaluations across multiple models and tasks on a 16\,GB RTX~5080 show lower memory usage and faster LoRA fine-tuning with competitive accuracy, enabling model adaptation on resource-constrained consumer hardware.

quick_skim.title: Heuristic-Driven Resource Optimization for Decoupled Memory Channels on FPGAs
quick_skim.abstract: Determining OpenCL channel depths for Decoupled Access-Execute (DAE) architectures in High-Level Synthesis (HLS) is critical for balancing performance and hardware efficiency. Conventional static analysis tools often over-provision these memory channels to ensure performance safety, leading to significant resource stranding. This paper presents an expansion of an LLVM-based static analysis framework, originally proposed for automated DAE generation, by introducing a hardware-aware refinement layer. We identify a counter-intuitive Performance Inversion Paradox linked to baseline memory stalls, where high-stall, grid-based kernels reach peak performance at minimal channel depths and suffer up to a 61% throughput degradation when depths are increased. We propose a Heuristic Refinement Layer that optimizes OpenCL channel depths based on this correlation between baseline stalls and performance saturation. Experimental results demonstrate that our expanded framework successfully identifies the Minimal Peak Performance point across various benchmarks. By avoiding the performance traps of standard over-provisioning, we achieve a 2.52x improvement in Resource Efficiency for an illustrative HotSpot application. This approach maintains peak execution speedup while ensuring the leanest possible hardware profile, outperforming conservative tool-based static predictions.

quick_skim.title: The KV-Surgeon: Compensation-Aware Offline KV-Cache Compaction
quick_skim.abstract: Offline compaction of the key--value cache (KV-cache) reduces the cost of repeatedly querying a fixed context by constructing a smaller cache once and reusing it subsequently. The central challenge of compaction is deciding which cache entries to delete and which to retain. Existing methods score each candidate for deletion on its own, with the rest of the cache being held fixed. However, softmax renormalization of the attention operation couples these decisions in a nonlinear manner: removing one entry changes the attention weights of every remaining one. In this work, we introduce KV-Surgeon, which uses calibration data to take interactions into account in a tractable way. We derive a quadratic surrogate that admits closed-form expressions for jointly making the optimal greedy removal decision as well as compensation within the remaining entries. On QuALITY, LongHealth, and Long Code Arena, and at every evaluated compaction ratio, KV-Surgeon substantially advances the cost--accuracy Pareto frontier of dense and mixture-of-experts models from 4B to 30B parameters. At $50\times$ compaction, KV-Surgeon improves question-answering accuracy by up to four points over attention matching (Zweiger et al., 2026), the state of the art, at comparable cost. Lastly, we introduce an even faster variant, which also exceeds the state of the art while requiring only two fifths of its cost.

quick_skim.title: Superposed analog memory for vector storage in neural networks
quick_skim.abstract: The growing memory demands of artificial neural networks pose a major challenge for energy-efficient computing, particularly for models that rely on large collections of high-dimensional weight and embedding vectors. Conventional memory architectures store these vectors individually, requiring many memory cells per vector and limiting achievable storage density. Here we demonstrate an analog memory architecture that encodes multiple vectors in a distributed superposition within a single memory array. Individual vectors are recovered through in-memory matrix-vector multiplication, allowing the degree of superposition to be tuned to balance storage density against recall fidelity. This approach introduces a new scaling dimension for analog memory, in which effective storage density can be increased without a corresponding increase in the number of physical memory cells. The distributed representation also provides resilience to device-level noise. We implement the architecture on a prototype phase-change memory chip and experimentally evaluate it using embedding tables from deep learning recommendation models and large language models. The results demonstrate inference accuracy comparable to full-precision software baselines, establishing analog superposition as a promising route towards dense, energy-efficient memory for artificial intelligence.

quick_skim.title: A Hybrid GPU and Processing-Near-Memory Architecture with Shared DRAM for Efficient Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
quick_skim.abstract: The growing adoption of large language models (LLMs) has significantly increased the compute and memory demands of inference serving. A key challenge arises from the mismatch between compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decoding: when executed together, the two phases interfere, while separating them via prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation leads to substantial resource underutilization. Specifically, prefill leaves memory bandwidth underutilized, whereas decoding underutilizes compute resources. Prior approaches, such as GPU Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) partitioning, attempt to improve utilization by spatially dividing GPU resources. However, these approaches remain fundamentally limited, as memory-bound decoding still requires a large number of SMs to saturate bandwidth, reducing the compute resources available for prefill and resulting in an inherent trade-off. To address this limitation, we propose DuoPD, a hybrid PD-disaggregation architecture that integrates lightweight Processing-Near-Memory (PNM) units into the HBM logic die. Unlike prior PIM/PNM designs that rely on costly internal bandwidth scaling and offload only partial decoding operations, DuoPD enables full decoding execution on PNM by leveraging bandwidth sharing with the GPU over a shared HBM interface. This allows compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decoding to execute concurrently with minimal interference, improving both compute and memory utilization. To realize this design, we develop a compact PNM microarchitecture, a TSV-level bandwidth sharing mechanism, and a hierarchical data mapping scheme tailored for hybrid GPU-PNM execution. Evaluations on server-scale LLMs demonstrate that DuoPD achieves up to 2.23x higher end-to-end throughput than conventional PD-disaggregation.

quick_skim.title: Fault-Tolerant Offloading Framework for Real-Time Applications in Mobile Edge Computing
quick_skim.abstract: This paper studies a Deadline-constrained task Offloading and resource Allocation Problem (DOAP) in a backhaul-network-enabled Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) system with both bandwidth and computational resource constraints. The goal is to maximize the total inference accuracy improvement across all tasks. We formulate this problem, denoted as $\mathbf{P}$, as an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) problem and show it is NP-hard via a reduction from the maximum-weight three-dimensional matching problem. To address $\mathbf{P}$, we develop $\mathtt{FastSA}$, a linear-time $\frac{1}{10}$-approximation algorithm based on the local-ratio technique. To the best of our knowledge, $\mathtt{FastSA}$ provides the first constant-factor performance guarantee for backhaul-network-enabled DOAPs. In addition, we introduce a fault detection and recovery framework that enables robust MEC operation under backhaul link and edge server failures. Experiments using profiled image classification workloads and real-world taxi traces show that $\mathtt{FastSA}$ achieves an average accuracy improvement of $25.6\%$ over benchmark algorithms under fault-free conditions while maintaining the lowest runtime. Under fault-injected scenarios, our framework reduces performance degradation by an average of $12.8\%$, demonstrating its effectiveness in fault handling.
